evidence.claim: The South Fork John Day River Back Country Byway follows the river canyon for 50 miles, from Dayville to the northern boundary of Malheur National Forest.
evidence.quote: This gravelled Back Country Byway parallels the Wild and Scenic South Fork John Day River through its incised canyon for a distance of 50 miles from its northern terminus at Dayville to the northern border of Malheur National Forest to the south.

evidence.claim: The drive passes through Columbia River basalt canyons, old-growth ponderosa pine, Douglas and white fir, and roadside willows.
evidence.quote: This drive takes visitors through deep canyons of Columbia River Basalts, through stands of old growth ponderosa pines, Douglas and white fir, and willows that line the road.

evidence.claim: The gravel surface accommodates most passenger vehicles, though some sections narrow to a single vehicle’s width.
evidence.quote: This high-standard gravel road is suitable for most passenger vehicles; however, know that some stretches of this road are single-vehicle width.

evidence.claim: Beside the byway, Rockpile Ranch dates from the late 19th century and remains a working private ranch.
evidence.quote: This private ranch was established in the late 19th century and is still in operation today.

evidence.claim: Izee’s two-room schoolhouse served students until 1989; it now hosts community functions.
evidence.quote: there is a small two-room schoolhouse located in Izee, about 34 miles upstream from Dayville. The school was used until 1989, when it closed its doors to students. Now it is used for community functions.

evidence.claim: Begin at Dayville, where South Fork Road meets US 26 beside the confluence of the two rivers.
evidence.quote: at the confluence of the John Day River with the South Fork John Day River. U.S. Route 26 runs east–west through Dayville, and South Fork Road, which runs north–south along the smaller river, meets the larger highway in the city.

evidence.claim: Head south to Black Canyon East Trailhead, nine miles from town, then toward Izee, about 34 miles upstream, and the national forest boundary.
evidence.quote: Nine miles south of Dayville, the Black Canyon East Trailhead offers hiking access into the Black Canyon Wilderness.

evidence.claim: Head south to Black Canyon East Trailhead, nine miles from town, then toward Izee, about 34 miles upstream, and the national forest boundary.
evidence.quote: there is a small two-room schoolhouse located in Izee, about 34 miles upstream from Dayville.

evidence.claim: Two rivers and two roads meet at Dayville. The South Fork joins the John Day here, while north–south South Fork Road connects with east–west US 26.
evidence.quote: at the confluence of the John Day River with the South Fork John Day River. U.S. Route 26 runs east–west through Dayville, and South Fork Road, which runs north–south along the smaller river, meets the larger highway in the city.

evidence.claim: In the mid-19th century, a wagon road through Dayville connected The Dalles on the Columbia River with gold mines near Canyon City. It became The Dalles Military Road in about 1870.
evidence.quote: In the mid-19th century, Dayville was along the route of a wagon road, renamed The Dalles Military Road in about 1870, that connected The Dalles on the Columbia River with gold mines near Canyon City.

evidence.claim: The byway begins with the turn south onto South Fork Road, following the smaller river toward Malheur National Forest.
evidence.quote: From Dayville, Oregon : Turn south on South Fork Road; the back country byway begins here.

evidence.claim: Nine miles south of Dayville, Black Canyon East Trailhead provides a way into the Black Canyon Wilderness.
evidence.quote: Nine miles south of Dayville, the Black Canyon East Trailhead offers hiking access into the Black Canyon Wilderness.

evidence.claim: The wilderness lies in the Ochoco National Forest, within the South Fork John Day River’s drainage basin.
evidence.quote: The Black Canyon Wilderness in the Ochoco National Forest lies within the river's drainage basin.

evidence.claim: Along the byway, the river cuts through Columbia River basalt, with ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, white fir and willows beside the drive.
evidence.quote: This drive takes visitors through deep canyons of Columbia River Basalts, through stands of old growth ponderosa pines, Douglas and white fir, and willows that line the road.

evidence.claim: Izee takes its name from a cattle brand: a local rancher marked his animals with the letters I. Z.
evidence.quote: Izee is a ranching community and was so named because a rancher there branded his cattle with the letters I. Z.

evidence.claim: The ranching community stands on the South Fork John Day River. Its post office operated from 1889 to 1954.
evidence.quote: Its post office operated from November 6, 1889, to July 31, 1954, and the first postmaster was Carlos W. Bonham. Located on the South Fork John Day River, Izee is a ranching community

evidence.claim: The small, two-room schoolhouse continued teaching children until 1989. Its use changed after the last students left: the building now serves community functions.
evidence.quote: The school was used until 1989, when it closed its doors to students. Now it is used for community functions.

evidence.claim: The river’s recreational classification in the National Wild and Scenic River system covers 47 miles, a separate designation from the road’s Back Country Byway identity.
evidence.quote: A total of 47 miles (76 km) of the river, from the Malheur National Forest boundary to Smoky Creek, are classified "recreational" in the National Wild and Scenic River (NWSR) system

evidence.claim: At Dayville, a mid-19th-century wagon road connected The Dalles on the Columbia River with the gold mines near Canyon City.
evidence.quote: In the mid-19th century, Dayville was along the route of a wagon road, renamed The Dalles Military Road in about 1870, that connected The Dalles on the Columbia River with gold mines near Canyon City.

evidence.claim: Along the river, Izee Falls drops 56 feet, and the drive passes both Black Canyon Wilderness and Aldrich Mountain Wilderness Study Area.
evidence.quote: The river itself contains beautiful rapids and the Izee Falls, which drops 56 feet vertically. Along the way, you’ll pass the Aldrich Mountain Wilderness Study Area as well as the Black Canyon Wilderness

evidence.claim: Dayville’s post office also changed locations: its original site lay three miles west of the present city.
evidence.quote: The original site of the Dayville post office was 3 miles (5 km) west of the city's current location.
